difficultyRationale: The violation is visible directly in a short, familiar if/else chain without requiring a multi-step refactor to reason about.
explanation: OCP is violated here because a specific, foreseeable kind of change — a new payment type — cannot be accommodated without modifying `charge`, even though the existing branches are untouched by the new requirement. That is different from the code merely being long or using an exception; the test is whether a known future change requires edits to code that has nothing to do with it.

options.text: The method is too long, and OCP is violated whenever a method exceeds roughly ten lines, regardless of whether that length comes from one cohesive block of logic that will never need another branch or from a chain of branches that keeps growing every time a new payment type is added.
options.explanation: Length alone isn't an OCP concern; a ten-line if/else chain that will never gain a new branch has no OCP problem, while a five-line method that must be edited for every new case does. The issue here is specifically that a known, recurring kind of change forces modification.

options.text: Using `==` to compare `request.type()` is the violation, because enum comparisons should always use `.equals()`.
options.explanation: `==` is actually the idiomatic and safe way to compare Java enum constants, since each constant is a singleton; this is unrelated to OCP, which concerns how the class responds to new payment types, not which comparison operator is used.

options.text: Supporting `CRYPTO` requires editing `charge` and recompiling/retesting the whole class, even though credit card, PayPal and bank transfer behavior are unchanged — the class is not closed against a kind of change (adding a payment type) that the team already knows will recur.
options.explanation: Correct. A kind of change that is known to recur (new payment types) forces modification of code unrelated to that specific change, which is exactly the situation OCP is meant to prevent.

options.text: Throwing `UnsupportedOperationException` in the `else` branch is the violation, because that exception should never appear in application code.
options.explanation: The fallback exception is a reasonable guard against an unmapped type and is not itself an OCP problem; the violation is that adding a real, supported payment type still requires modifying this method, not that an exception type appears in one branch.
